results.authors: ter Horst L, Brouwer MC, van der Ende A, van de Beek D
results.summary: In a cohort of 53 adults with community-acquired bacterial meningitis and CSF leakage, 59% of episodes were recurrent. Rhinoliquorrhea was the predominant presentation (76%). Streptococcus pneumoniae caused 51% of cases, Haemophilus influenzae 17%. Outcome was favorable in 88%. Causes of CSF leakage included ENT surgery, remote head trauma, congenital defect, and neurosurgery. Expert consensus recommends investigation for underlying structural causes in all adults with recurrent bacterial meningitis.
results.title: Community-acquired Bacterial Meningitis in Adults With Cerebrospinal Fluid Leakage

results.authors: van de Beek D, de Gans J, Spanjaard L, et al.
results.summary: Recurrent bacterial meningitis is uncommon and always indicates an underlying predisposing condition. Common causes are anatomical defects (CSF fistula from trauma, surgery, congenital), followed by immune defects (antibody deficiency, complement deficiency, asplenia). Beta-2-transferrin assay on nasal or ear secretions is the standard diagnostic test for confirming CSF origin. High-resolution CT of the skull base with coronal reconstructions is first-line imaging to localise the bony defect. MRI with gadolinium (or intrathecal gadolinium-enhanced MRI) provides complementary soft tissue characterisation. Surgical repair reduces recurrence risk.
results.title: Recurrent Bacterial Meningitis — Systematic Approach to Finding the Cause

results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.summary: Empiric therapy: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone; dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h x4 days before or with first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT treat this second episode of pneumococcal meningitis in isolation without investigating for an anatomical or immunological predisposing cause — failure to do so guarantees further recurrence and potentially fatal episodes.
Do NOT delay empiric IV antibiotics while awaiting imaging or LP when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when altered mental status is present (imaging-first criterion per IDSA 2004).

Do NOT attribute the chronic unilateral watery rhinorrhea to allergic rhinitis without beta-2-transferrin testing — the reservoir sign and unilateral clear rhinorrhea in the context of recurrent meningitis demand CSF-leak confirmation.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV + ceftriaxone 2 g IV) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion — do NOT delay for imaging or LP beyond what is strictly required for safety.

Draw two sets of blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.
Collect nasal secretion sample for beta-2-transferrin assay to confirm CSF rhinorrhea as the anatomic portal.
Perform CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status); request skull-base bone-algorithm reconstructions to characterise the cribriform plate defect.
Send full CSF panel at LP: cell count/differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, multiplex PCR, and CSF lactate.

Investigate the predisposing cause of recurrence: skull-base CT with bone algorithm AND gadolinium MRI to characterise the defect; send quantitative immunoglobulins and CH50 to exclude humoral/complement deficiency.
Arrange ENT and neurosurgical consultations for elective endoscopic skull-base repair of the cribriform plate defect after acute infection is controlled, to prevent further recurrence.
Administer conjugate pneumococcal vaccine (PCV20 or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) and meningococcal vaccine after recovery.

key_clinical_evidence: Recurrent bacterial meningitis is not a random event — it ALWAYS requires investigation for an anatomical defect (CSF fistula) or an immune defect (antibody deficiency, complement deficiency, asplenia); treating each episode in isolation is a serious omission.

Beta-2-transferrin assay on nasal secretions is the gold-standard diagnostic test for CSF rhinorrhea, with sensitivity >90% and near-perfect specificity; positive result confirms the nasal discharge is CSF.

The 'reservoir sign' (increased rhinorrhea on leaning forward) and unilateral constant clear watery discharge, especially in the context of prior head trauma, are cardinal features of CSF rhinorrhea that must not be attributed to allergic rhinitis without confirmatory testing.

Skull-base CT with high-resolution bone-algorithm coronal reconstructions is first-line imaging to localise the bony defect and guide surgical planning; MRI with gadolinium provides complementary soft tissue characterisation and detects meningoencephalocele.
Normal immunoglobulins and CH50 effectively exclude CVID and terminal complement deficiency as the predisposing cause, making the anatomical defect the unifying diagnosis in this case.
Adjunctive dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg IV q6h x 4 days), given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose, reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
Definitive prevention of further recurrence requires surgical repair of the cribriform plate defect (typically endoscopic endonasal approach) combined with pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

metadata.condition_name: Recurrent acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with CSF rhinorrhea from left cribriform plate defect
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: each isolated episode looks like routine community-acquired pneumococcal meningitis. The critical clue — second episode within 14 months plus a 3-year history of positional clear left-sided rhinorrhea previously attributed to allergic rhinitis — is the pivot that should trigger a structured anatomical/immunological workup. The agent must recognise the recurrence pattern, connect the rhinorrhea to a CSF leak, order beta-2-transferrin and skull-base imaging, exclude immune causes, and recommend surgical referral — rather than simply treating the acute episode and discharging.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required tools; 3 embedded red herrings (rhinorrhea misdiagnosed as allergic rhinitis, anchoring on isolated-episode framing, sinusitis as alternative focus); requires cross-modality synthesis (CSF + CT + MRI + immune labs + literature) to diagnose both the acute infection and the underlying anatomical predisposition; normal immune workup means the puzzle has only one unifying answer (structural defect).
metadata.real_seed_note: Clinical pattern seeded from published literature on recurrent bacterial meningitis with CSF leak (ter Horst et al., Clin Infect Dis 2019, PMID 31300817; CC-BY-NC-ND open access) and supporting case reports (PMC5551538, PMID 28819362, CC-BY). No single published case was reproduced verbatim. The case was authored de novo with distinct demographics (28-year-old South Asian male), a left cribriform plate defect post minor head trauma, a 14-month inter-episode interval, and an explicitly normal immune workup, making the anatomical defect the sole demonstrated predisposing cause. The diagnostic puzzle (overlooked CSF rhinorrhea attributed to allergic rhinitis) and the recurrence flag as the key pivot are consistent with epidemiological and case-report data from the cited sources.
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response

patient.history_present_illness:
A 28-year-old South Asian man presents to the emergency department with an 18-hour history of rapidly progressive severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and fever. This is his second episode of bacterial meningitis within 14 months. His first episode occurred 14 months ago at another hospital, where he was admitted with an identical syndrome of fever, headache, and meningismus and was diagnosed with Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis by CSF culture. He was treated with 14 days of IV ceftriaxone, recovered fully, and was discharged with no further workup to identify an underlying predisposing cause. At that time, neither a skull-base CT nor an immunological workup was performed, and no follow-up with an ENT or neurosurgeon was arranged.

For the past three years, the patient has had chronic intermittent clear watery discharge from the left nostril. He had been evaluated by an allergist approximately 18 months ago, was skin-tested and found to have mild sensitisation to house dust mite, and was diagnosed with allergic rhinitis. Antihistamines and an intranasal corticosteroid were prescribed. He describes the nasal discharge as 'like water' and notices it is especially prominent when he bends forward or tilts his head, and when he lies flat. He reports that it is always unilateral, left-sided, and clear — it has never been purulent. He did not connect this symptom to his episode of meningitis 14 months ago. He has a history of a minor motorcycle accident at age 24, which caused a mild head injury; a CT brain at that time was reported as normal, but no dedicated imaging of the skull base was performed.

The current episode began yesterday morning with a diffuse, rapidly worsening headache that he rated 10 out of 10 within hours. He developed neck stiffness that prevented him from touching his chin to his chest. Fever was documented by thermometer at 39.0 degrees Celsius at home. He developed severe photophobia and nausea. He presented to the ED approximately 8 hours after symptom onset. On arrival, he immediately recognised the syndrome as identical to his prior episode. He has not taken any antibiotics in the week prior to presentation. He is otherwise healthy with no chronic medical conditions, no immunosuppressive medications, and no sick contacts.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked nuchal rigidity present — passive neck flexion restricted and painful. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. No petechiae, purpura, or skin rash. Nasal examination by ER physician: watery clear discharge noted from the left naris, more prominent with the patient leaning forward (positive reservoir sign). No lymphadenopathy.
